parts: John Baird is generally regarded as the father of television. The BBC began the first television service in 1936 and is the world's oldest television broadcaster; US broadcasts began in 1939; other countries began on a wide scale in the 1950s; the Second World War slowed development. Early broadcasts were black and white; the first successful colour programme was transmitted by CBS in the USA in 1953. Television moved from 'radio with pictures' to its own style in a 'golden age'.

Television began in India on 15 September 1959 as an experiment under All India Radio with two one-hour programmes a week for school children and farmers, with community sets around Delhi. By the 1970s television centres opened elsewhere. In 1976 Doordarshan became a separate department independent of AIR. SITE (Satellite Instructional Television Experiment), August 1975 to July 1976, used the American satellite ATS-6 to broadcast educational programmes to Indian villages in six states, twice a day, on agriculture, health, family planning, with entertainment (dance, music, drama, folk art). In 1982 the Ninth Asian Games gave Doordarshan national coverage for the first time through the satellite INSAT 1A and the first colour transmission. In 1983 government sanctioned a huge expansion of Doordarshan (serials Hum Log, Buniyaad, Nukkad); by the end of the 80s about 75 per cent of the population were covered. In 1997 Prasar Bharati was established as a statutory autonomous public service broadcaster for AIR and DD. Today about 90 per cent can receive Doordarshan, with around 30 channels (DD National, DD News, DD Sports, DD Gyandarshan, DD Bharati, Loksabha Channel, DD Urdu, regional channels).

In the 1990s private channels ended Doordarshan's monopoly. The coverage of the Gulf War by the American news channel CNN propelled satellite television in India; STAR (Satellite Television Asian Region) agreement with an Indian company gave Zee TV, the first privately owned Hindi satellite channel. The Supreme Court ruling of 1995 said airwaves are not the monopoly of the government. Regional channels: Sun TV (Tamil), Asianet (Malayalam), Eenadu TV. International channels: CNN, BBC, Discovery. Categories: news, religious, cartoon and movie channels.

Positive: an excellent teacher and mass education medium (SITE), opens new horizons, creates awareness about issues such as environmental pollution and global warming, entertainment and relaxation. Negative: advertisements tempt children to nag for products; 'couch potato' (people who spend most time in front of TV) distracts from reading, sports and chores and may lead to obesity; stereotypes (an oversimplified standardized image of a person or group, e.g. women shown inside the house); violence linked with aggression and acceptance of violence, especially in children who have experienced violence, poverty or neglect; fear in children. Television is neither good nor bad; its effect depends on how we use it.

Delivery: terrestrial transmission (antenna, the traditional method), cable networks (broadcaster to cable operator to homes; free-to-air channels such as Aaj Tak, Sahara and Times Now, and pay channels like Sony and Star Plus charging per subscriber) and direct broadcast satellite (DTH). New platforms: mobile TV broadcasting and Internet Protocol Television (IPTV), which allows watching, recording and sharing television on computers and mobile phones with an internet connection and a set-top box. Challenge from new media (interactivity): audience-backed shows where the audience decides the winner, and reality television (Indian Idol, Big Boss, Sa Re Ga Ma Pa). A disadvantage of television is delayed feedback, while the internet is interactive.
